excerpt_original: An off-site exhibition by the Institut pour la photographie in Lille, Bérangère Fromont’s “République” (Republic) explores daily life on a square known for its uprisings, somewhere between friendly encounters and gentle resistance. L’article “République”: Everyday Revolts est…

blocks.text: Begun in 2023, the series “République” unfolds exclusively on the Paris square of the same name, extending a body of work on the notion of resistance that Bérangère Fromont has been developing for several years. The site is symbolic: in the collective imagination, it is the place of great popular gatherings, of revolts and revolutions. Yet the photographs, hosted by the Théâtre du Nord in Lille at the initiative of the Institut pour la photographie, do not openly speak of rebellion. Instead, a strange softness emanates from the monochromes and rich grays of the images hung on the theater’s white walls. They show bodies, those of young people (skaters in particular) who make the square their own, day after day. Bare-chested bodies, resting bodies, bodies that brush against and touch one another. The grain of the prints, delicately nuanced, becomes almost sensual. It sets portraits and architectural details in dialogue, like so many sculptural figures to contemplate.

blocks.text: “Bérangère Fromont carried out this project with a singular technique. She immersed herself in the square, going there every day at the end of the afternoon. She shot wide, with an 80mm lens and no zoom, then extracted details that she enlarged,” explains Florentine Bigeast, communications manager at the Institut. These elements, lifted from the wide frescoes she captures, are then printed with particular care, in piezography (using carbon ink) on a mulberry-fiber paper that is both thin and resilient. This refinement allows the subjects to seize the viewer’s gaze. Set against reworked black backgrounds, as if to underline their contours, they shift from anonymous figures to protagonists of a subtle narrative.

blocks.text: “The photographer maintains that speaking about resistance through a project of apparent gentleness does not soften the message; on the contrary, it underscores it,” notes Florentine Bigeast. Rooted in a space heavy with symbolism (Place de la République evokes a well-known chapter of French history, but also recalls the many squares of the same name in other cities, which often mark the starting point of a demonstration), the project becomes compelling for what it leaves unsaid, for what it does not show. Here, skin is velvety, eyes are closed, shoulders relaxed. And yet “République” invites us to ask: where are the women in these pictures? What does their near-absence say about their place in public space? How is resistance expressed today? Can a peaceful revolt exist? How can these places be occupied outside moments of active protest?

blocks.alt: Black-and-white photograph of two young men in white T-shirts seen from behind, trees in the background, Place de la République, Paris
blocks.caption: République © Bérangère Fromont, Courtesy Galerie Bacqueville

blocks.text: At a time when high school students’ demonstrations, harshly repressed by the police, raise more than ever the question of young people’s role in a form of revolution, Bérangère Fromont’s exhibition reminds us that engagement also arises, sometimes, in the most ordinary actions.
“République” is on view at the Théâtre du Nord , Lille, through January 16, 2027.
